title: Error Handling
subtitle: try/catch in async code, process-level handlers, and operational vs programmer errors
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: Unhandled errors crash Node.js processes. In async code, errors can be swallowed silently or crash the process at unexpected points. Without a clear error handling strategy, debugging becomes extremely difficult.
whyItExists.solution: Always await async operations inside try/catch. Distinguish operational errors (expected: file not found, network timeout) from programmer errors (bugs: null reference, type error). Handle operational errors gracefully. Let programmer errors crash — they reveal bugs.
whyItExists.whenToUse: Every async function that can fail. Every HTTP handler. Every file operation. Every external service call.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't catch errors you can't handle meaningfully — let them propagate up to a layer that can. Don't use empty catch blocks that swallow errors silently.

explainModes.beginner: In Node.js, errors in async code need try/catch around await expressions. If you don't catch an error, the promise rejection goes unhandled and Node.js prints a warning (or crashes in newer versions). Wrap await calls in try { const result = await something(); } catch (err) { console.error(err.message); }.
explainModes.simple: try/catch with async/await: works just like sync try/catch — the await unwraps the rejected promise into a thrown error. Promise.reject(): add .catch() if not awaiting. process.on('unhandledRejection', handler): catches any forgotten .catch(). process.on('uncaughtException', handler): catches sync throws outside try/catch. Error types: err.code ('ENOENT', 'ECONNREFUSED') for system errors. Custom error: class NotFoundError extends Error { constructor(msg) { super(msg); this.name = 'NotFoundError'; this.statusCode = 404; } }.
explainModes.standard: Operational vs programmer errors: Operational = expected failures (file missing, network down, invalid user input, resource limit). Handle gracefully — return 404, retry, log and continue. Programmer = bugs (TypeError, undefined is not a function, assertion failure). These should crash — they reveal bugs that need fixing, not handling. Error middleware in Express: (err, req, res, next) — 4 args, catches errors passed to next(err) or thrown in async handlers. Async Express wrappers: asyncHandler(fn) pattern — wraps async routes to catch rejections and forward to next(err).
explainModes.technical: process.on('unhandledRejection', (reason, promise) => {}): fires when a Promise rejects and has no .catch handler. In Node.js 15+, defaults to crashing the process (same as uncaughtException). process.on('uncaughtException', (err, origin) => {}): fires for sync throws not inside any try/catch. Best practice: log, clean up, then exit — don't try to resume. AggregateError: wraps multiple errors (Promise.any rejects with this). err.cause: chain errors with new Error('message', { cause: originalError }) — preserves the original error for debugging while adding context.
explainModes.deepDive: Error boundary pattern: define clear error domains. HTTP layer catches and translates errors to HTTP status codes. Business logic layer throws typed errors (ValidationError, NotFoundError, ConflictError). Data layer throws database errors. Each layer adds context via err.cause. Structured logging: log error objects (stack, code, context) as JSON for log aggregators (Datadog, Elastic). Never log sensitive data in errors. Correlation IDs: attach a request ID to errors so distributed traces can link log lines across services. Sentry / Bugsnag: capture unhandled errors in production, group by type, alert on spikes.

content.text: Never write an empty catch block: `catch (err) {}`. If you don't handle an error, at least log it with `console.error(err)`. Silent error swallowing is one of the hardest bugs to debug.

questions.question: What is the difference between an 'operational error' and a 'programmer error' in Node.js?
options: Operational errors are thrown by the OS; programmer errors are thrown by npm packages

Operational errors are expected failures (file not found, network timeout, invalid user input) that should be handled gracefully. Programmer errors are bugs (TypeError, null dereference) that should crash the process.
Operational errors only happen in production; programmer errors only happen in development
Operational errors use the Error class; programmer errors use a special OperationalError class
questions.explanation: Operational errors are things you can anticipate and handle: a database connection failing, a file being missing, invalid user input. You catch these and respond gracefully (return 404, retry, show an error message). Programmer errors are bugs in your code — accessing a property on null, calling undefined as a function. These should crash the process because continuing to run after a bug can lead to data corruption or unpredictable behavior. The distinction helps you decide whether to catch an error or let it propagate.

faq.q: My async function throws an error but nothing happens — why?
faq.a: You likely called the async function without await and without .catch(). The promise rejects silently. Always do one of: (1) `await asyncFn()` inside a try/catch, (2) `asyncFn().catch(handleError)`, or (3) listen to `process.on('unhandledRejection', ...)` as a safety net. In Node.js 15+, unhandled rejections crash the process — so 'nothing happens' in older Node versions but crashes in newer ones.

examples: Express error middleware — central error handler that formats errors as JSON API responses
Prisma database errors — .code field (P2002 = unique constraint, P2025 = record not found)
Axios network errors — err.response for HTTP errors, err.request for network errors, no response for other errors
